rounds.proof_sketch: The kernel is launched with dim3 block(inner_size), meaning threadIdx.x ranges from 0 to inner_size-1. Therefore inner_idx = threadIdx.x can NEVER equal or exceed inner_size. Original condition (inner_idx >= inner_size) is always FALSE. Mutant condition (inner_idx > inner_size) is also always FALSE. Both expressions are logically equivalent across all possible thread indices.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the early-return guard from 'inner_idx >= inner_size' to 'inner_idx > inner_size'. However, CUDA thread indexing guarantees that threadIdx.x ranges from 0 to blockDim.x-1, and the kernel is launched with blockDim.x = inner_size. This means inner_idx (which equals threadIdx.x) has a maximum value of inner_size-1. Since inner_idx can never reach inner_size, both 'inner_idx >= inner_size' and 'inner_idx > inner_size' always evaluate to false for all threads that are actually launched. The guard condition difference has no observable effect on execution.
rounds.kill_strategy: The mutant is unkillable under any value-level testing because the predicate boundary is architecturally unreachable. CUDA's thread indexing model ensures threadIdx.x is always strictly less than blockDim.x, making both comparison operators equivalent when checking against the block dimension. No input values can change this fundamental property of CUDA thread scheduling.
rounds.recommendations: When writing bounds checks in CUDA kernels, understand that checks like 'threadIdx.x >= blockDim.x' are inherently dead code since CUDA guarantees threadIdx.x < blockDim.x. Mutation testing tools should recognize such patterns as equivalent mutations and skip them, or the original code should be refactored to remove unreachable guards that only serve documentation purposes.
